groups.high: An extension cord's printed current, voltage and wattage ratings define its permitted use; do not exceed them. Ratings vary, so 13 A at 125 V, or 1,625 W, is an example, not a universal household specification. Add the loads of all connected appliances and account for starting surges where relevant. The relationship watts = volts × amps gives the stated example for a suitable load, but motor and AC power characteristics may require more detailed information. Excess current heats conductors and can damage insulation, causing fire or shock. Length, wire size, damage, ventilation and operating conditions also affect safe use. Keep cords uncovered, out from under rugs and free from pinching. Use an outdoor-rated cord where required, and never use a damaged one or connect multiple extensions in series. High-power appliances such as portable heaters should follow their own direct-outlet instructions. Extension cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for adequate fixed outlets; ask a qualified electrician when unsure.
groups.mid: Read the rating on your extension cord. Do not exceed its amp, volt or watt limits. Some cords are rated 13 A at 125 V, which gives 1,625 W. That is an example, not a rule for every cord. Add up the loads of all devices plugged into it. Motors may draw extra power when starting, so check the device instructions too. Too much current heats the wires. It can melt insulation and cause fire or shock. A long, thin or damaged cord can add risk. Keep cords uncovered and out from under rugs. Do not pinch them with furniture or join several extensions in a chain. Use a cord made for outdoor use if needed. Stop using damaged cords. High-power heaters may need a direct wall connection, as their instructions state. An extension cord is for temporary use. It does not replace proper fixed outlets. Ask a qualified electrician if you are unsure which cord or outlet is safe.
groups.low: Check the label on an extension cord before use. Do not go over its amp, volt or watt rating. A cord marked 13 A at 125 V may be rated 1,625 W. Other cords have different limits. Add the power used by all the devices on the cord. A motor may need more when it starts. Check its guide. Too much current can overheat the wires, melt the insulation and cause fire or shock. Long, thin or damaged cords can add risk. Keep the cord out from under rugs and do not cover it. Do not trap it under furniture or link several cords together. Use an outdoor-rated cord outside. Do not use a damaged cord. A high-power heater may need to plug straight into a wall socket. Follow its guide. Extension cords are temporary, not a way to replace fixed outlets. Ask a qualified electrician if you do not know what is safe.
groups.source_review: Checked CPSC cord capacity, damage, placement and fire prevention guidance.
groups.notes: Qualified 1625W example; removed invented universal temperatures, thermal equilibrium and at-rating prohibition.

groups.high: For long-term lithium-ion device storage, follow the manufacturer's instructions. A partly charged state around 50% is commonly recommended; 40–60% is a useful approximate range, not a universal safety law that begins at exactly 30 days. Apple advises about 50% charge, switching the device off and storing it in a cool, dry place below 32°C. For storage longer than six months, it advises recharging to about 50% every six months. Other products may specify different intervals or temperatures. A completely depleted battery may discharge further and become unusable; prolonged full-charge storage, especially in heat, can accelerate capacity loss. Avoid hot vehicles, moisture and physical damage. Do not bypass a protection circuit or attempt to revive a deeply discharged, swollen, leaking or damaged battery yourself. Use the recommended charger and seek appropriate service or recycling. Check stored devices periodically under their own care guidance rather than assuming one fixed self-discharge rate or per-cell voltage suits every battery.
groups.mid: Follow the maker's guide when storing a lithium-ion battery device for a long time. About half charge is often advised. A range of 40–60% is a rough guide, not a law that starts at exactly 30 days. Apple says to charge to about 50%, switch off and keep it in a cool, dry place below 32°C. For more than six months in storage, Apple says to recharge to about 50% every six months. Other products may have different rules. A fully empty battery can drain further and stop working. A full battery left in heat may lose capacity faster. Keep it out of hot cars and away from moisture or damage. Use the recommended charger. Do not bypass safety circuits or try to revive a deeply drained, swollen, leaking or damaged battery yourself. Seek service or safe recycling. Check the device from time to time under its own guide. One fixed discharge rate or cell-voltage limit does not fit all batteries.
groups.low: Store a lithium-ion device as its maker says. Half charge is often best for a long break. About 40–60% is a rough guide. It is not a rule that starts at 30 days. Apple says about 50% charge. Switch the device off and keep it cool and dry, below 32°C. If stored for more than six months, Apple says to charge it to about 50% every six months. Other makers may give other advice. A flat battery can drain too far and stop working. A full battery left in heat may hold less charge later. Keep it out of hot cars and away from damp or damage. Use the right charger. Do not bypass its safety circuit. Do not try to fix a swollen, leaking, damaged or deeply drained battery yourself. Ask for service or safe recycling. Check it from time to time as the maker says. One discharge rate or cell-voltage limit does not fit all batteries.
groups.source_review: Checked Apple official storage instructions; product-specific rather than universal lithium chemistry mandate.
groups.notes: Removed fabricated exact 30-day onset, universal discharge/voltage and equilibrium claims.

groups.high: IP67 describes an enclosure's ingress protection under IEC 60529. The first digit, 6, means dust-tight under the specified test; the second, 7, concerns temporary water immersion. For many small consumer devices, manufacturers describe the test as immersion in fresh water up to 1 metre for 30 minutes. These are laboratory conditions, not a promise of permanent waterproofing in every environment. The exact test geometry and product instructions matter. IP67 alone does not establish resistance to high-pressure jets, salt water, soap, hot water or swimming. Dust-tight and waterproof are not interchangeable claims. Seals can deteriorate through wear or damage, so check the manufacturer's care and warranty terms. Do not deliberately test a damaged device or charge it while wet. IP65 concerns a different water-jet test; IP68 immersion conditions are specified by the manufacturer and do not translate into unlimited underwater use. Choose protection for the actual environment rather than treating the last digit as a general guarantee.
groups.mid: IP67 is an ingress-protection rating under IEC 60529. It describes tests of a device's outer case. The 6 means dust-tight under the test. The 7 means protection during temporary immersion in water. Many small devices use a fresh-water test of up to 1 metre for 30 minutes. Check the product's own terms because test conditions and device size matter. IP67 is not a promise of permanent waterproofing. It does not by itself cover high-pressure jets, salt water, soap, hot water or swimming. Dust-tight does not mean safe in all liquids. Seals may weaken with wear or damage. Follow the maker's care and warranty advice. Do not test a damaged device in water or charge it while wet. IP65 refers to a water-jet test. IP68 uses immersion conditions set by the maker, not a right to stay underwater without limit. Choose a rating for the real use rather than relying on one number alone.
groups.low: IP67 tells you how a device's case was tested. It comes from IEC 60529. The 6 means dust-tight in that test. The 7 means it can handle temporary immersion in water. For many small devices, the test uses fresh water up to 1 metre deep for 30 minutes. Read the maker's exact terms. Size and test conditions matter. This is not a promise that it is always waterproof. IP67 alone does not cover strong water jets, salt water, soap, hot water or swimming. Keeping dust out is not the same as being safe in every liquid. Wear and damage can weaken seals. Follow the care guide and check the warranty. Do not put a damaged device in water to test it. Do not charge it while wet. IP65 is a water-jet test. IP68 has water limits set by the maker. It does not mean unlimited underwater use. Pick a device for how you will really use it.
groups.source_review: IEC page blocked (403); checked manufacturer explanation of IEC-based IP67 tests. Full paid IEC test text not independently retrieved.
groups.notes: Removed unconditional orientation, immediate void-on-drop and universal IP68 depth/duration claims; acknowledged test limitations.

groups.high: Secure a home router by changing default administrative credentials and setting a separate, long, unique Wi-Fi passphrase. The router login controls settings; the Wi-Fi passphrase controls joining the wireless network. Prefer WPA3-Personal where supported, or WPA2 with AES when compatibility requires it. Avoid WEP and obsolete WPA/TKIP. A minimum of 12 characters is not a guarantee against guessing; current CISA advice favours at least 16 characters, using randomness or a phrase of unrelated words. Do not reuse passwords or rely on predictable substitutions. Apply firmware updates, disable unnecessary remote administration and WPS, and follow the manufacturer's setup instructions. Save the new credentials securely. Changing the Wi-Fi passphrase usually requires reconnecting devices, although behaviour varies by product. Review connected devices and guest-network settings. Packet capture or intrusive scanning is not necessary for ordinary household setup and should never target networks without permission. Strong credentials reduce risk but do not eliminate software flaws, phishing or every method of compromise.
groups.mid: Change the router's default admin login and set a long, unique Wi-Fi passphrase. These are two different passwords. The admin login changes settings. The Wi-Fi passphrase lets devices join. Use WPA3-Personal if supported, or WPA2 with AES when needed for older devices. Do not use WEP or old WPA/TKIP. Twelve characters is not a promise of safety. CISA now advises at least 16 characters, made at random or from unrelated words. Avoid reused passwords and easy patterns. Update the router's firmware, the software inside it. Turn off remote admin and WPS if you do not need them. Follow the maker's guide and keep the new passwords safe. After a Wi-Fi password change, devices will usually need to reconnect. Check which devices are linked and review guest access. You do not need packet capture or intrusive scans for a normal home setup. Never test networks without permission. Strong passwords cut risk, but cannot prevent every flaw, scam or attack.
groups.low: Your router has two kinds of login. The admin password lets you change settings. The Wi-Fi passphrase lets devices join. Change the default admin login. Use a long, unique Wi-Fi passphrase too. Choose WPA3-Personal if the router supports it. If needed, use WPA2 with AES. Do not use WEP or old WPA/TKIP. A 12-character password is not a promise of safety. CISA advises at least 16 characters. Use random text or a phrase of unrelated words. Do not reuse passwords or use easy patterns. Update the router's firmware, its built-in software. Turn off remote admin and WPS if not needed. Follow the maker's guide and keep passwords safe. Devices will usually need to reconnect after a Wi-Fi password change. Check which devices are linked and who has guest access. Normal home setup does not need packet capture or intrusive scans. Never test a network without permission. Strong logins help, but do not stop every flaw or scam.
groups.source_review: Checked CISA home wireless/password guidance; 16-character recommendation identified as contemporary advice.
groups.notes: Corrected 256^N/12-character guarantees and conflated admin/Wi-Fi credentials; removed unnecessary external scanning instructions.

groups.high: Class 3B lasers can cause serious eye injury from a direct beam or mirror-like reflection; do not rely on the roughly 0.25-second blink response for protection. The often-quoted 5–500 mW range describes certain continuous-wave visible-laser classifications, not every wavelength or pulsed source. A competent laser-safety assessment must consider wavelength, power, pulse characteristics, exposure and beam geometry. Prioritise enclosures, beam stops, interlocks, restricted access, warning signs and trained operation. Where exposure remains possible, use laser protective eyewear selected for the correct wavelength range and optical density; ordinary sunglasses and generic goggles are not substitutes. Eyewear is personal protective equipment, not an engineering control, and cannot justify deliberately looking into a beam. Keep reflective objects out of the beam path and follow the local laser safety officer's procedures. Seek prompt medical assessment after suspected eye exposure. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 addresses bloodborne pathogens, not the claimed Class 3B eyewear rule; applicable obligations depend on the setting and relevant standards.
groups.mid: A Class 3B laser can seriously damage eyes through its direct beam or a mirror-like reflection. Do not rely on a blink to protect you. The roughly 0.25-second blink response may be too slow. The 5–500 mW range applies to some continuous visible lasers, not every colour or pulsed laser. A trained safety person must assess the wavelength, power, pulses and possible exposure. Enclose the beam where possible. Use beam stops, interlocks, warning signs and controlled access. Train everyone who may be exposed. If exposure is still possible, use laser eyewear chosen for the right wavelength and optical density. Ordinary sunglasses or general goggles are not enough. Eyewear is personal protection, not an engineering control. Never look into a beam just because you have goggles. Remove shiny objects from the beam path and follow the laser safety officer's rules. Seek prompt medical care after suspected eye exposure. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 is about bloodborne pathogens, not the stated laser-eyewear rule. The actual safety duties depend on the setting.
groups.low: A Class 3B laser can badly hurt your eyes. The direct beam and mirror-like reflections are dangerous. A blink is not enough to keep you safe. Its roughly 0.25-second response may be too slow. The 5–500 mW range is for some continuous visible lasers. It is not a rule for every wavelength or pulsed beam. Ask a trained laser-safety person to check the power, wavelength, pulses and exposure. Use an enclosed beam where possible. Use beam stops, interlocks, signs and limits on access. Staff need training. If exposure is possible, wear laser goggles with the right wavelength range and optical density. Normal sunglasses or general goggles will not do. Goggles are personal protection, not an engineering control. Do not look into the beam while wearing them. Keep shiny objects out of its path. Follow the laser safety officer's rules. Get medical help promptly after suspected eye exposure. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 covers bloodborne pathogens, not that laser rule. Real duties depend on the setting.
groups.source_review: Checked OSHA laser classification/hazard guidance and control hierarchy; historical 5–500mW scope qualified.
groups.notes: Corrected false bloodborne-pathogen citation, classification generalisation and PPE/engineering-control confusion.

groups.high: Never mix household chlorine bleach with ammonia or ammonia-containing cleaners. The mixture can release toxic chloramine vapours that irritate the eyes and airways and may cause severe lung injury. Bleach mixed with acids can release chlorine gas, so do not combine bleach with other cleaning products unless the label explicitly directs a safe preparation. Read labels, keep products in original labelled containers and use appropriate ventilation and protective equipment. Store incompatible products so leaks cannot mix. If accidental mixing produces fumes, leave the area immediately for fresh air and keep others away. Do not re-enter to clean up or attempt chemical neutralisation. A household mask is not adequate protection against hazardous gases. Call emergency services for breathing difficulty, collapse or significant exposure, and contact a poison service for substance-specific advice. In the United States, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222. Only trained responders should undertake hazardous-atmosphere rescue or administer oxygen under appropriate protocols. Symptoms can worsen after exposure, so follow medical advice even if initially mild.
groups.mid: Never mix bleach with ammonia or cleaners that contain it. The mixture can release toxic chloramine fumes. These can hurt the eyes and lungs and may cause severe breathing injury. Bleach mixed with acids can release chlorine gas too. Do not mix cleaning products unless a label gives clear instructions for a safe preparation. Read labels, keep products in their original marked bottles and use good ventilation. Wear protection stated on the label. Store products so leaks cannot mix. If fumes form after a mix, leave at once for fresh air and keep others away. Do not go back to clean it up or add another chemical to cancel it out. A household mask will not protect you from these gases. Call emergency services for breathing trouble, collapse or a serious exposure. Ask a poison service for advice. In the US, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Hazardous rescue and oxygen treatment are for trained staff. Symptoms may get worse later, so follow medical advice even if they seem mild.
groups.low: Never mix bleach with ammonia. Some cleaners contain ammonia, so read the label. The mix can make toxic chloramine fumes. They can hurt eyes and lungs and cause severe breathing trouble. Bleach and acids can make chlorine gas too. Do not mix cleaners unless the label tells you how to do so safely. Keep them in their own labelled bottles. Use fresh air and the protection on the label. Store them so leaks cannot mix. If you mix them and fumes appear, get out to fresh air now. Keep others away. Do not go back to clean it up. Do not add a chemical to fix it. A home mask will not stop these gases. Call emergency help for breathing trouble, collapse or serious exposure. Call a poison service for advice too. In the US, Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222. Only trained staff should enter dangerous gas or give oxygen. Signs may get worse later. Follow medical advice even if you feel better.
groups.source_review: Checked CDC/NIOSH no-mixing guidance and fresh-air emergency response.
groups.notes: Removed speculative explosive byproduct description and unsafe lay re-entry/respirator/oxygen instructions.

groups.high: A three-prong appliance designed for protective grounding should be used with a correctly wired grounding connection. The equipment-grounding conductor provides a fault-current path back to the source so a protective device can disconnect a fault; it is not simply a drain into soil. Never remove the grounding pin or use an ungrounded adaptor to defeat protection. A metal casing can become live if an internal fault occurs, and both 120 V and 230 V supplies can cause fatal shock. Shock severity depends on current path, duration and conditions, not voltage alone or a safe 0.6-second threshold. Proper grounding reduces risk but does not guarantee that no current can pass through a person. A GFCI or RCD provides additional protection and is not the same as an equipment ground. Some legally compliant ungrounded replacement arrangements require specific protection and labelling; a qualified electrician should assess them. Approved double-insulated appliances may legitimately have two-prong plugs. Have damaged cords, missing pins, uncertain outlets or suspected faults checked rather than modifying wiring yourself.
groups.mid: Use a three-prong appliance with the grounding connection it was designed for. The ground wire gives fault current a path back to the supply so a fuse or breaker can cut the power. It does not just send electricity into the soil. Never cut off the ground pin or defeat it with an ungrounded adaptor. A fault can make a metal case live. Both 120 V and 230 V can cause fatal shock. Harm depends on the path and time of current through the body and other conditions, not voltage alone. There is no safe 0.6-second contact rule. Grounding reduces risk but cannot promise zero current through a person. A GFCI or RCD adds protection, but is not an equipment ground. Some ungrounded replacement outlets are allowed only with specific protection and labels. Ask an electrician to assess them. Approved double-insulated appliances can safely use two-prong plugs as designed. Have damaged cords, missing pins or uncertain outlets checked. Do not change wiring yourself.
groups.low: A three-prong appliance needs the ground it was made to use. A ground wire gives fault current a path back to the supply. This helps the fuse or breaker cut power. It is not just a path into soil. Do not cut off the ground pin. Do not bypass it with an ungrounded adaptor. A fault can make a metal case live. Both 120 V and 230 V can kill. The path and time of current through the body matter too. There is no safe 0.6-second rule. Grounding helps, but does not promise no shock. A GFCI or RCD gives extra protection. It is not the same as a ground wire. Some old ungrounded outlets can be replaced only under special rules for protection and labels. Ask an electrician to check. Some approved double-insulated tools have two-prong plugs by design. They are not missing a ground pin. Get damaged cords, missing pins and unknown outlets checked. Do not alter the wiring yourself.
groups.source_review: Checked OSHA grounding and double-insulated exceptions; GFCI distinction qualified by local code.
groups.notes: Corrected all-two-prong-dangerous claim, universal grounding mandate, guaranteed zero casing voltage and unsafe timing threshold.

groups.high: HVAC filters should be checked and serviced according to the equipment and filter manufacturer's instructions. A dirty filter can restrict airflow, impair heating or cooling performance and increase energy use. Many disposable filters are changed roughly every 1–3 months, but dust, pets, smoke, operating hours and filter design can require a different interval. Some filters are washable rather than disposable. Do not assume every HEPA filter lasts 6–12 months or can be installed in any system: a dense filter can cause excessive pressure drop in equipment not designed for it. Use the specified size, airflow direction and efficiency rating, and obtain technical advice before increasing filtration substantially. Switch the system off before accessing the filter and refit the cover safely. Check more often during heavy use. Clean-filter energy savings depend on the system and conditions; the claimed universal 15% penalty is not established by the reviewed material. Maintain filters for appropriate airflow and indoor air quality rather than relying on one calendar or a guaranteed saving.
groups.mid: Check your HVAC filter using the system and filter maker's guide. A dirty filter can block airflow, reduce heating or cooling and raise energy use. Many throwaway filters need changing about every 1–3 months. Dust, pets, smoke and heavy use can mean sooner. Other filter designs may last longer or need washing instead. Do not assume all HEPA filters last 6–12 months. Do not fit a dense HEPA filter to a system that cannot handle it. Too much resistance can reduce airflow. Use the right size and efficiency rating, with the airflow arrow the right way. Ask a technician before a large change in filter type. Switch the system off before opening the filter cover and put it back safely. Check more often when the system runs a lot. Energy savings vary with the system and the dirt. The reviewed material did not establish a fixed 15% penalty for every dirty filter. Follow the real maintenance needs, not one calendar or promised saving.
groups.low: Check the HVAC filter as the maker says. HVAC means heating, ventilation and air conditioning. Dirt can block the flow of air. This can reduce heating or cooling and use more energy. Many throwaway filters need changing in 1–3 months. Dust, pets, smoke and heavy use may mean a shorter time. Some filters can be washed. Others last longer. HEPA filters do not all last 6–12 months. A dense HEPA filter may not suit your system. It can block too much air if the system is not built for it. Use the right size and type. Point the airflow arrow the right way. Ask a technician before a big change in filter type. Switch off before you open the cover. Put the cover back safely. Check more often in heavy use. Savings vary by system and dirt level. A fixed 15% penalty for every dirty filter was not confirmed. Follow the maker's guide, not one set date or promise.
groups.source_review: DOE legacy maintenance URL returned 404 in this pass. Manufacturer-dependent interval retained as qualified general guidance; universal HEPA and 15% figures not claimed verified.
groups.notes: Removed universal HEPA interval and fixed efficiency/energy penalty; source retrieval limitation explicitly recorded.

groups.high: Do not heat sealed or airtight containers in a microwave. Steam and expanding contents can raise pressure until the container bursts, causing scalds or injuries from hot material. Use microwave-safe cookware and vent lids or coverings as directed; loosen a lid or leave a corner open rather than sealing it tightly. Follow both food-packaging and oven instructions, and avoid metal unless the manufacturer explicitly permits its use. Even microwave-safe containers may become hot from the food, so use suitable protection when handling them. Let standing time elapse and open coverings away from the face and hands to release steam safely. Liquids can also become superheated and erupt when disturbed even without a sealed lid. Follow recommended heating times and take care moving heated liquids. Venting reduces pressure risk but does not eliminate every microwave burn hazard. Do not use an oven with a damaged door or faulty interlock; stop if it operates with the door open and seek service.
groups.mid: Do not heat a sealed container in a microwave. Steam and expanding food can build pressure until it bursts. Hot food, liquid and steam can cause severe burns. Use microwave-safe dishes and let steam escape as the guide says. Loosen the lid or leave a corner of the cover open. Do not seal it tight. Follow the food pack and oven instructions. Avoid metal unless the oven maker says it is allowed. A microwave-safe dish may still get hot from the food. Protect your hands. Allow the stated standing time, then open covers away from your face and hands. Even an open cup of water can become superheated and erupt when moved. Do not heat liquids longer than the guide recommends, and move them with care. A vent cuts pressure risk, but cannot prevent every burn. Do not use an oven with a damaged door or faulty safety switch. If it runs with the door open, stop using it and seek service.
groups.low: Never heat a sealed container in a microwave. Steam and expanding contents build pressure that can burst the container. Hot food, liquid and steam can burn you badly. Use a dish marked microwave-safe. Let steam out as the guide says. Loosen the lid or leave one corner of the cover open. Do not seal it tight. Read the food pack and oven guide. Do not use metal unless the oven maker allows it. A safe dish can still get hot from food, so protect your hands. Wait for the stated standing time. Open the cover away from your face and hands. Water can become superheated even in an open cup and may erupt when disturbed. Use the recommended heating time and move hot drinks with care. A vent helps, but does not stop all burns. Do not use an oven with a damaged door or safety switch. Stop if it runs with the door open and get it serviced.
groups.source_review: Checked FDA microwave-safe containers, superheated-liquid and damaged-door precautions; USDA venting guidance.
groups.notes: Removed false implosion/exponential pressure guarantees and venting-eliminates-risk overclaim.

groups.high: Wheel fasteners must be tightened to the exact torque specified for the vehicle, wheel and fastener combination. Torque is a turning moment, commonly measured in lb-ft or N·m. The quoted 80–100 lb-ft range may suit some applications but is not a universal specification. Under-tightening can allow movement and loosening, potentially leading to wheel separation. Over-tightening can damage threads or studs and impair correct clamping. Use a suitable, accurate torque wrench and the manufacturer's staged or star-pattern sequence. Follow instructions about clean threads, lubrication and replacement fasteners; adding lubricant when the specification assumes dry threads can alter clamp force. Do not rely on an impact tool alone to set final torque. Follow the model-specific recheck interval; some Ford manuals specify rechecking within 100 miles after wheel removal, but this is not a universal 50–100-mile rule. Calibration and inspection intervals depend on the wrench and use. If unsure, have a qualified technician perform the installation rather than choosing a generic value.
groups.mid: Use the exact wheel-nut torque in your vehicle's guide. It must suit the wheel and fasteners too. Torque means turning force, measured in lb-ft or N·m. The 80–100 lb-ft range fits some uses, not every car. Too loose can let the wheel move and nuts work free. The wheel could come off. Too tight can damage threads or studs and weaken correct clamping. Use an accurate torque wrench and the tightening order the maker gives. This may use stages and a star pattern. Follow rules for clean threads, oil and replacement parts. Do not add oil if the torque assumes dry threads; it can change the force on the joint. Do not use an impact tool alone for final torque. Follow the vehicle's recheck time. Some Ford guides say within 100 miles after wheel removal, but not all cars use that rule. Check and calibrate the wrench as its maker requires. If unsure, ask a qualified technician rather than guessing a number.
groups.low: Find the exact wheel-nut torque in your vehicle guide. It must match the wheels and fasteners. Torque is turning force, given in lb-ft or N·m. Do not assume 80–100 lb-ft fits every car. Too loose, and nuts can work free. A wheel could come off. Too tight, and threads or studs can be damaged. This can spoil the clamping force too. Use a proper, accurate torque wrench. Tighten in the order and stages the maker gives, often a star pattern. Follow the rules for clean threads and the right parts. Do not add oil if the number is for dry threads. Oil changes how much the joint is clamped. An impact tool alone is not enough to set final torque. Check again when the vehicle guide says. Some Ford guides say within 100 miles after a wheel is removed. Other cars may differ. Follow the wrench's own care and calibration guide. Ask a qualified technician if you are not sure. Do not guess.
groups.source_review: Checked Ford model-specific owner manuals, clean-thread and recheck instructions; no universal torque asserted.
groups.notes: Corrected blanket 80–100 lb-ft rule and universal annual calibration/50–100-mile recheck claims.
